This is the heart of Rust. Everything else in the language follows from these three rules. Read this module twice.

The three rules

  1. Every value has exactly one owner.
  2. There can only be one owner at a time.
  3. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped (its destructor runs, its memory is freed).

That is it. Memory safety, no garbage collector, no use-after-free, no double free — all of it falls out of these three rules plus the borrow rules below.

Move semantics

In C++, let s2 = s1 would be a copy (or a move that leaves s1 "valid but unspecified"). In Rust the compiler tracks it and rejects use after move.

Copy vs move

Types that are cheap to duplicate implement Copy and are copied instead:

Copy Not Copy
all integers, floats, bool, char String, Vec<T>, Box<T>
&T (shared references) &mut T
tuples/arrays of Copy types most structs by default

Rule of thumb: derive Copy only for small, plain-data types (≤ 4 words). A Copy struct containing a 1 KB array silently copies on every assignment, and you will not see it in the code.

Cloning is explicit

Clone is visible at the call site. That is the point: allocation costs are never hidden.

Borrowing

Moving everything in and out of functions would be unbearable. Instead, borrow:

The borrow rules

At any point in time, for a given value, you may have either:

  • any number of shared borrows (&T), or
  • exactly one mutable borrow (&mut T),

but never both at once. And references must always be valid (no dangling).

Violating it:

Why this rule exists

It eliminates data races at compile time. A data race requires two threads accessing the same memory, at least one writing, without synchronisation. If a &mut T cannot coexist with any other reference, that situation cannot be expressed. Send/Sync (module 02.10) extend the same argument across threads.

Non-lexical lifetimes (NLL)

Borrows end at their last use, not at the end of the block:

This is why Rust code from 2015 looked so contorted and modern Rust does not.

&mut is not "mutable reference" in the C++ sense

&mut T means exclusive access. It is a guarantee to the compiler that nobody else can see this value, which is why the optimiser can do so much.

Method receivers

Pick the weakest receiver that works: &self unless you must mutate, self only when the type is a one-shot builder or converter.

Lifetimes

A lifetime is how long a reference is valid. You mostly do not write them — the compiler infers them via elision rules. You write them when the compiler cannot tell which input a returned reference came from.

The problem

The compiler asks: the returned reference — is it tied to a or to b? It cannot know, so it refuses.

Read 'a as: "there is some region 'a such that both inputs live at least that long, and the output lives no longer than that." The returned reference is valid for the shorter of the two inputs.

Elision rules

The compiler applies three rules, in order:

  1. Each elided input lifetime becomes its own parameter.
  2. If there is exactly one input lifetime, it is assigned to all elided outputs.
  3. If there is a &self or &mut self parameter, its lifetime is assigned to all elided outputs.

Lifetimes in structs

A struct holding a reference needs a lifetime parameter:

Rule of thumb: if you find yourself adding lifetimes to a struct, ask whether it should own the data (String instead of &str). Structs with lifetimes propagate that parameter into every type that uses them. For domain types, owning is almost always simpler.

'static

'static means "valid for the entire program". String literals are 'static. A 'static bound on a trait object or thread also means "contains no borrows":

Gotcha: 'static does not mean "leaked" or "lives forever in RAM". It means "no shorter lifetime could invalidate it". Box::leak gives you one, but so do all literals, and neither costs anything at runtime.

Common borrow-checker fights, and the real fix

1. Mutating while iterating

Fixes, in order of preference:

2. Returning a reference to a local

Fix: return owned (String), or take the storage as a parameter (fn fill(buf: &mut String)).

3. Two &mut into the same Vec

splice_at_mut, iter_mut, chunks_mut, split_at_mut exist precisely to express "two disjoint mutable pieces".

4. Self-referential structs

Do not build these. Options: store indices instead of slices, use owning_ref/yoke/self_cell, or restructure so the borrow is local.

5. Storing a borrow in a struct that outlives the source

Symptom: error[E0597]: does not live long enough. The fix is nearly always "make the struct own a String/Arc<str>".

Interior mutability: the escape hatch

When you need to mutate through a shared reference, use Cell/RefCell (single-threaded) or Mutex/RwLock/atomics (multi-threaded). The borrow rules are then checked at runtime instead of compile time. Details in Smart pointers.

A worked example: a text buffer with borrowed views

lines_with returns Vec<Line<'a>> where 'a is the lifetime of doc. The compiler proves the vector cannot outlive the document. Zero copies, zero allocation beyond the Vec itself.

Exercises

  1. Write fn longest_word(s: &str) -> &str. Why does this compile without an explicit lifetime? Which elision rule applies?
  2. Write fn first_of(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str returning whichever is non-empty. Add the lifetime annotation. Then call it where b is a temporary and observe the error.

  4. Write a struct WordIndex<'a> holding Vec<&'a str> of unique words. Then rewrite it to own Vec<String> and compare the API ergonomics.
  5. Implement fn split_twice(s: &mut Vec<i32>) -> (&mut [i32], &mut [i32]) using split_at_mut. Call it and mutate both halves.
